paragraphs: Training a support vector machine involves both fitting the model and choosing its settings. This paper brings those operations together in a consolidated cross-validation procedure for kernel SVMs. Its aim is to reduce the computation needed to train and tune these models while retaining essentially the same predictive accuracy.

The method combines an exact leave-one-out formula with a data reduction strategy. Leave-one-out evaluation considers how a model performs when individual examples are held out. The formula provides a foundation for consolidating that evaluation, while data reduction accelerates the underlying SVM computation. These two ingredients address the combined training and tuning workload.

The authors also introduce a two-stage version that handles an intercept, a model component not supported by the existing data reduction methods discussed in the abstract. Numerical studies report roughly a tenfold speed improvement over kernlab and LIBSVM, with almost unchanged accuracy. The result is an empirical improvement in computational efficiency for the studied settings, including models with an intercept.
neurips-2022-a-consolidated-cross-valida.tldr: A consolidated cross-validation method uses data reduction to train and tune kernel SVMs roughly ten times faster in numerical studies, with almost unchanged accuracy.

paragraphs: Recovering a complete ranking becomes difficult when pairwise comparisons are noisy: an item can lose a comparison even when it belongs higher in the ordering. This paper studies exact ranking without assuming Strong Stochastic Transitivity, a structural property that restricts how comparison probabilities relate across items.

The proposed algorithm, Probe-Rank, actively chooses comparisons to learn the ordering. It is delta-correct, meaning its probability of returning an incorrect ranking is controlled by the chosen error tolerance delta. The main theoretical result bounds the number of comparisons using only preference probabilities between items that are neighbors in the true ranking.

This dependence matters because earlier bounds involve probabilities for every pair, allowing comparisons between distant items to affect the stated difficulty. The new bound improves those results and supports advantages over a large collection of instances that violate Strong Stochastic Transitivity. Numerical experiments across several settings also find substantially greater sample efficiency than the state-of-the-art active ranking method used for comparison.
neurips-2022-active-ranking-without-stro.tldr: Probe-Rank learns exact rankings from noisy comparisons with guarantees depending only on neighboring items, without requiring Strong Stochastic Transitivity.

paragraphs: A segmentation model trained on labeled synthetic scenes must recognize image regions in real scenes whose appearance it has never encountered. This paper studies that synthetic-to-real generalization problem. The authors find that image style strongly affects performance and that channel-wise means and standard deviations can represent style features well.

Their method, AdvStyle, treats these style features as parameters that can be changed during training. Adversarial updates produce difficult styles, which are then used to construct training images. The model therefore practices on challenging appearance variations generated dynamically, helping prevent it from fitting too closely to the style of its synthetic source data.

Experiments on two synthetic-to-real segmentation benchmarks report significant improvements on unseen real domains and state-of-the-art performance. The authors also apply the approach to domain-generalized image classification and find improvements on the datasets considered. Because the augmentation operates through style features, the paper presents it as straightforward to implement and applicable to different models. The findings support style variation as a useful target for improving generalization.
neurips-2022-adversarial-style-augmentat.tldr: AdvStyle generates challenging image styles during training to improve synthetic-to-real segmentation and generalization to unseen domains.

paragraphs: In asynchronous stochastic gradient descent, parallel devices can supply gradient updates after the model has already changed. Earlier analyses become much less favorable when even one update is heavily delayed. This paper argues that those bounds give an overly pessimistic picture of how delays affect the algorithm.

The authors establish stronger guarantees for the same asynchronous SGD algorithm that depend on the number of parallel devices rather than on gradient delays. Their analysis combines delay-adaptive step sizes with a new recursion involving virtual iterates. These virtual iterates provide an analytical sequence through which the behavior of delayed updates can be studied.

The results cover both convex and nonconvex objectives and improve strictly on the existing analyses described in the abstract. The authors also argue that asynchronous SGD outperforms synchronous minibatch SGD in the settings they consider. The contribution is therefore a sharper theoretical account of parallel optimization: large delays need not make the available guarantees collapse, and device count can provide a more useful basis for describing performance.
neurips-2022-asynchronous-sgd-beats-mini.tldr: A sharper analysis gives asynchronous SGD guarantees based on device count rather than gradient delays and supports advantages over synchronous minibatch SGD in the studied settings.

paragraphs: Conditional image synthesis often has several plausible outputs for one input, even though training provides only one example output. A useful generator must capture that variety while producing convincing images. This paper addresses the tendency of GAN-based methods to miss possible outputs, commonly called mode collapse.

The approach builds on Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or IMLE. It uses the same kind of generator as a GAN but replaces adversarial training with an objective that places a generated sample near every observed image. Earlier IMLE methods need many samples to obtain high fidelity. Conditional Hierarchical IMLE, or CHIMLE, is designed to achieve that fidelity without requiring so many samples.

The paper reports improved fidelity and mode coverage across night-to-day translation, 16-fold super-resolution, colorization, and decompression. Average FID improves by 36.9% against the prior best IMLE method and 27.5% against the best non-IMLE general-purpose methods in the comparison. These results support the method's ability to combine realistic outputs with broader coverage of possible images across the four evaluated tasks.
neurips-2022-chimle-conditional-hierarch.tldr: CHIMLE reduces the sampling burden of IMLE while improving image fidelity and output diversity across four conditional image synthesis tasks.

paragraphs: Representation meta-learning usually searches for one representation that many tasks can share. That arrangement can be restrictive when different kinds of tasks need different features. This paper studies a conditional alternative in which the representation itself changes according to information available about the task being solved.

The method learns a conditioning function that maps task side information, potentially the task's own training dataset, to a tailored linear representation. The authors analyze environments where this strategy improves over standard meta-learning. One example is an environment with separate task clusters, where tasks within each cluster share a representation but a single representation does not capture all clusters equally well.

The paper then proposes a meta-algorithm intended to realize this conditional advantage in practice. It also obtains a benefit in the unconditional setting: a new estimator with faster learning rates and fewer hyperparameters to tune than the state-of-the-art methods considered. Preliminary experiments support the results. The contribution links task-dependent representations to identifiable task structure while also improving the shared-representation case.
neurips-2022-conditional-meta-learning-o.tldr: Learning a task-conditioned linear representation can improve meta-learning in structured task environments, with preliminary experiments supporting the theory.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small substitute for a dataset that approximately retains structure needed for computation. Running a learning algorithm on that substitute can reduce its cost. Conventional construction methods, however, assume that the full input dataset is already available explicitly, which can be a demanding requirement for relational data.

Here, the data is spread across multiple tables. Joining those tables to construct a complete learning matrix can itself be expensive, before the learning algorithm even begins. The paper proposes an aggregation tree with pseudo-cube approach that builds a coreset from the bottom up, addressing coreset construction within this relational setting.

The approach also circumvents several difficulties associated with relational learning, according to the abstract. Under assumptions described as mild, the authors show that it can support tasks including clustering, logistic regression, and support vector machines. The contribution makes the organization of the input data part of the efficiency problem: reducing the learning workload is more useful when obtaining the reduced dataset does not first require the expensive full join.
neurips-2022-coresets-for-relational-dat.tldr: A bottom-up coreset construction supports learning from relational tables without first requiring an expensive fully materialized data matrix.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains an outer learning problem that depends on an inner optimization problem. This paper studies how a network of agents can solve such problems when each agent communicates only with its neighbors. That restriction makes the spread of information through the network part of the optimization challenge.

The proposed algorithm uses gossip-based communication and updates both optimization levels on a single timescale. Agents share information locally, allowing it to propagate through the network. For K agents and accuracy parameter epsilon, the paper proves per-agent sample complexity of order 1/(K epsilon²) for general nonconvex bilevel problems and 1/(K epsilon) for objectives satisfying the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.

These bounds give a linear improvement with network size in the stated sample complexity, and the paper establishes optimal dependence on both K and epsilon. Simulated experiments in hyperparameter tuning and decentralized reinforcement learning report state-of-the-art training efficiency and test accuracy. Together, the results show how local communication can support statistically efficient cooperation on nested optimization problems.
neurips-2022-decentralized-gossip-based-.tldr: A gossip-based bilevel optimizer achieves optimal per-agent sample complexity with linear scaling benefits from the number of networked agents.

paragraphs: A visual counterfactual explanation changes an image enough to change a classifier's decision while keeping the edit small and realistic. The aim is to make the decision change understandable through image content. This paper develops diffusion-based counterfactuals for arbitrary ImageNet classifiers, addressing restrictions and unrealistic artifacts in earlier approaches.

One part of the method controls how much the image changes. An adaptive parameterization uses hyperparameters that transfer across images and models, while distance regularization and a late start to diffusion keep the generated image close to the original. Together, these components seek a different classification with minimal semantic alteration.

A second component, cone regularization, uses an adversarially robust model to guide the diffusion process away from trivial changes that lack semantic meaning. Thus, the classifier being explained need not itself be robust, although a robust model still contributes to generation. The resulting explanations are described as realistic images of the target class that receive high confidence from the classifier, linking the changed decision to visible content.
neurips-2022-diffusion-visual-counterfac.tldr: Diffusion-based counterfactuals use controlled image changes and robust-model guidance to explain decisions of arbitrary ImageNet classifiers.

paragraphs: Long-range LiDAR detection becomes costly when a detector builds dense feature maps over the area it observes. The paper describes their computation and storage costs as growing quadratically with perception range. Its Fully Sparse Detector, or FSD, instead has costs roughly linear in the number of points and independent of range itself.

FSD combines a sparse voxel encoder with a sparse instance recognition module. This module first groups points into object instances, then extracts features and makes predictions for each instance. That organization resolves the missing-center-feature issue that obstructs fully sparse center-based or anchor-based detection. It also avoids the expensive neighbor queries used by earlier point-based approaches.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on the Waymo Open Dataset and examine how the detector works. The authors also evaluate Argoverse 2, whose 200-meter range exceeds Waymo's 75 meters. In that longer-range setting, FSD reports state-of-the-art performance and runs 2.4 times faster than its dense counterpart. The results connect the sparse design to a practical efficiency gain at larger perception ranges.
neurips-2022-fully-sparse-3d-object-dete.tldr: FSD groups LiDAR points into instances for fully sparse detection, achieving state-of-the-art results and a 2.4-fold speed advantage in the evaluated long-range setting.

paragraphs: Classification with rejection allows a model to abstain when an example is difficult to classify, reducing the risk of a consequential wrong prediction. Earlier methods with theoretical guarantees support only certain loss functions. This paper develops a formulation that allows more flexible loss choices while providing a theoretical basis for learning.

The central result rewrites a K-class rejection problem as a classification problem with K+1 classes on the original data distribution. The extra class represents the rejection option. The authors use this equivalence to construct an empirical risk minimization method and derive an estimation error bound for it.

They also identify necessary and sufficient conditions for consistency of surrogate losses built from classification-calibrated multiclass losses. Here, consistency means that minimizing the training surrogate leads to minimizing the intended rejection-aware risk. This distinction matters: flexibility in selecting a loss comes with precise conditions connecting optimization to the desired decision rule. Benchmark experiments support the method's effectiveness, complementing the equivalence, error bound, and consistency characterization.
neurips-2022-generalizing-consistent-mul.tldr: Recasting rejection as an additional class enables flexible loss functions with explicit error bounds and conditions for consistent learning.

paragraphs: This paper combines two kinds of pretrained language models to learn language-understanding tasks without task-specific data. A text-generating model creates examples, and a bidirectional model learns to classify them. The setup uses generation as a source of training material for a separate understanding model.

Prompts guide the generator to produce text associated with particular classes. The method selects training examples using their generation probabilities, then fine-tunes the bidirectional model on the selected synthetic data. Label smoothing and temporal ensembling are applied during fine-tuning to improve generalization and stability. These steps make data selection and the learning procedure both part of the approach.

Across seven GLUE classification tasks, the method substantially outperforms the zero-shot prompting methods evaluated. It also produces results comparable to strong few-shot approaches given 32 training examples per class. The result shows that, in these evaluations, zero-shot task learning can benefit from an intermediate synthetic dataset and model fine-tuning. Zero-shot here refers to the absence of task-specific data, even though the second model undergoes training.
neurips-2022-generating-training-data-wi.tldr: Prompt-generated training examples let a bidirectional language model achieve strong zero-shot classification results without task-specific data.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards from an expert's behavior. The difficulty is that multiple reward functions can produce the same optimal policy. Observing several experts with different discount factors or environments can resolve that ambiguity under certain conditions, identifying rewards up to an additive constant.

This paper gives an equivalent identifiability statement for multiple experts in tabular Markov decision processes using an easily checked rank condition. The condition is also necessary, so it characterizes when recovery is possible in the analyzed setting. The authors extend their results to rewards expressed as linear combinations of known features and to cases with approximate transition matrices.

The paper separately studies whether expert behavior can support an optimal agent in a new environment when the reward itself remains ambiguous. It supplies conditions characterizing when that generalization is possible. This separates two questions that need not have the same answer: whether one can recover the reward and whether one can act optimally elsewhere. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical results on both questions.
neurips-2022-identifiability-and-general.tldr: The paper characterizes when multiple experts identify a reward function and when their behavior supports optimal transfer even without reward identifiability.

paragraphs: In a dynamic system, treating one experimental unit can affect others through a shared constraint, such as limited product supply. This interference complicates the estimation of intervention effects. The paper formulates this Markovian interference problem as policy evaluation, bringing reinforcement-learning tools to the analysis of experiments.

The authors introduce the Differences-In-Q's estimator, an on-policy alternative to off-policy evaluation. Off-policy estimators are unbiased but can carry a large variance cost relative to existing heuristics. The new estimator can have exponentially smaller variance, while its bias is second order in the size of the intervention's impact.

That combination gives a specific bias–variance tradeoff: it accepts a controlled form of bias in exchange for potentially substantial reductions in variability. The authors report that this tradeoff lets the estimator effectively dominate state-of-the-art alternatives. Their empirical evaluation includes experiments in a city-scale ride-hailing simulator. The theoretical development also introduces three techniques of independent interest to reinforcement learning, connecting practical interference estimation to broader policy-evaluation questions.
neurips-2022-markovian-interference-in-e.tldr: The Differences-In-Q's estimator addresses dynamic experimental interference with second-order bias and potentially exponentially lower variance than off-policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning uses a fixed dataset to learn both environmental dynamics and a rewarding policy. Uncertainty in the learned dynamics creates a tension between exploiting the model and avoiding unreliable predictions. The paper argues that converting this uncertainty into reward penalties can produce unintended tradeoffs because rewards and dynamics play different roles.

The proposed approach maintains a distribution over possible dynamics and evaluates policies using samples biased toward pessimistic possibilities. An alternating Markov game formulation supplies the sampling rule. The authors show that this procedure induces a revised dynamics belief whose reweighting depends on the policy, which they call Pessimism-Modulated Dynamics Belief.

For policy improvement, the paper develops an iterative regularized optimization algorithm with a monotonic improvement guarantee under a stated condition. A practical offline algorithm then approximately solves the game. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmark tasks. The contribution places pessimism directly in how possible environmental dynamics are considered, with theory for the game and empirical support for the practical approximation.
neurips-2022-model-based-offline-reinfor.tldr: Pessimism-Modulated Dynamics Belief handles offline model uncertainty by biasing dynamics sampling, with conditional policy-improvement guarantees and strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn how to reach many goals using only previously collected data. GoFAR formulates this as matching state occupancy: the states visited by an agent constrained by real dynamics should match those of an imagined expert that can move directly to the goal.

From this perspective, the authors derive a regression-based learning algorithm. GoFAR does not require hindsight relabeling, and its value and policy networks can be optimized without interleaving their updates. The paper attributes improved offline performance and stability to these features and provides a statistical performance guarantee unavailable to the prior methods considered.

The same objectives can also train an agent-independent goal-conditioned planner from offline source-domain data, enabling zero-shot transfer to new target domains. Experiments across tasks report substantial improvements over prior state-of-the-art approaches. In a real robotic dexterous manipulation task, GoFAR learns complex behavior that achieves diverse goals while the comparison methods make no meaningful progress. These findings support both the goal-reaching formulation and its extension to planning.
neurips-2022-offline-goal-conditioned-re.tldr: GoFAR learns goal-reaching behavior from offline data through state-occupancy matching, with strong experimental results and an extension to transferable planning.

paragraphs: This paper learns policies for multiple agents from an existing dataset, without collecting additional online experience. It casts the learning problem as sequence modeling, allowing the framework to build on the Transformer architecture. The design combines centralized learning from the dataset with separate policies that agents can execute independently.

Training begins with a teacher policy that treats the multi-agent dataset as though it came from one agent. The teacher identifies and recombines useful behavior within that data. Separate student policies are then created for the individual agents and trained through knowledge distillation from the teacher.

The transfer includes both the teacher's features and the structural relationships among features belonging to different agents. This makes relationships across agents part of the knowledge passed to the decentralized policies. On several environments, the method outperforms the state-of-the-art model-free offline multi-agent baselines evaluated and is more robust to demonstration quality. The results support sequence modeling and relational distillation as a practical combination for learning coordinated behavior from fixed data.
neurips-2022-offline-multi-agent-reinfor.tldr: A centralized Transformer teacher distills behavior and relationships into separate agent policies, improving offline multi-agent learning in the evaluated environments.

paragraphs: Learning across multiple populations can require protecting the population with the highest loss, rather than optimizing an overall average. This paper studies that worst-case objective over n predefined distributions. The setting encompasses collaborative learning, fair federated learning, and group distributionally robust learning, with sample efficiency as the central question.

The authors establish optimal sample complexity and give algorithms that attain it. Their bounds exceed the cost of learning from one distribution by only an additive term of n log(n)/epsilon², where epsilon is the accuracy parameter. This describes how the statistical cost of covering multiple distributions enters the guarantee.

The algorithms learn which distributions to sample and learn from on demand. Their design extends stochastic optimization techniques to zero-sum games in a new stochastic setting. The resulting bounds improve earlier guarantees for agnostic federated and collaborative learning and provide the first sample complexity bounds for the group DRO objective considered. The contribution links adaptive data collection to optimal guarantees for a shared worst-case learning goal.
neurips-2022-on-demand-sampling-learning.tldr: On-demand sampling achieves optimal sample complexity for minimizing the worst-case loss across multiple predefined distributions.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives each agent its own objective, measured on its local data distribution. This paper focuses on many agents that individually have very little data. The central question is how many samples the agents collectively need to approximately minimize the generalization error of one specified agent.

The authors prove matching lower and upper sample bounds and give strategies that attain them. These strategies filter and combine stochastic gradients received from other agents. They rely on prior information about a notion of distance between agents' local distributions, using that information to decide how outside gradients should contribute.

The method balances bias and variance: information from other distributions can reduce sampling noise while also moving learning away from the target agent's own objective. The matching bounds establish that the proposed balance is sample-optimal in the studied setting. The paper also quantifies what happens when distribution distances are only roughly estimated from very few local samples, connecting the idealized prior information to a data-limited version of the problem.
neurips-2022-on-sample-optimality-in-per.tldr: Filtering other agents' gradients using distribution-distance information achieves matching sample-complexity bounds for personalized learning with scarce local data.

paragraphs: Parallel tempering samples a difficult posterior by connecting it to a reference distribution through intermediate distributions. The reference is often the prior. When prior and posterior have almost no overlap, however, this construction can become prohibitively expensive. The paper improves the connection by adapting the reference to the posterior.

The reference is tuned to minimize forward KL divergence using gradient-free moment matching. The authors prove convergence of the adaptation to the forward KL minimizer and show that this divergence is a useful proxy for an established measure of parallel-tempering performance. A generalized annealing path connects the fitted reference to the target posterior.

For typical Bayesian models in the large-data limit, the paper shows improving performance for the proposed method while traditional parallel tempering deteriorates arbitrarily. It also introduces a split path with both a fixed and a variational reference to stabilize adaptation. Experiments across realistic Bayesian inference scenarios report large gains. The results make reference selection and adaptation central to the efficiency of the sampling procedure.
neurips-2022-parallel-tempering-with-a-v.tldr: Adapting a variational reference with moment matching makes parallel tempering substantially more efficient in the analyzed models and evaluated inference scenarios.

paragraphs: Video restoration can process many frames together or handle them sequentially. Joint processing combines temporal information well but can demand large models and substantial memory. Frame-by-frame recurrence shares parameters efficiently, yet has weaknesses in parallel processing and long-range dependency modeling. RVRT combines these approaches within one restoration architecture.

The model divides a video into clips. Neighboring frames inside each clip are processed in parallel, with their features updated jointly. Across clips, a recurrent structure uses features inferred for the previous clip to help estimate the next. This arrangement combines local parallel processing with information carried through the video.

Guided deformable attention aligns information between clips by predicting multiple relevant locations in the previously inferred clip and aggregating their features through attention. Experiments cover video super-resolution, deblurring, and denoising. The paper reports state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets alongside a balance of model size, testing memory, and runtime. The contribution is a concrete architectural compromise between restoration quality and the resources required to combine information across frames.
neurips-2022-recurrent-video-restoration.tldr: RVRT combines parallel processing within clips and recurrent attention across clips to restore video with strong quality and balanced resource use.

paragraphs: One explanation for convolutional networks' vulnerability to adversarial examples is their reliance on high-frequency image information. Earlier frequency analyses often divide the spectrum manually and draw qualitative conclusions. This paper develops a finer quantitative approach using Shapley values, a contribution measure from cooperative game theory.

The method measures whether individual frequency components help or hurt the network's behavior. Its analysis reveals differences across individual examples, making the picture more detailed than a single broad claim about high-frequency reliance. The authors also examine adversarial training and attacks statistically in the frequency domain.

These observations motivate hypotheses about why adversarial training improves robustness, how its effects differ across classes, and which frequency components attacks favor. The abstract presents these as hypotheses arising from analysis, rather than established universal explanations. The authors then use Shapley values to guide a data augmentation method. Image-classification benchmark experiments support its effectiveness at improving robustness, connecting a more detailed account of frequency contributions to a practical training intervention.
neurips-2022-rethinking-and-improving-ro.tldr: Shapley values quantify frequency contributions to CNN behavior and guide an augmentation method that improves robustness in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness can require substantial model capacity, creating tension with compact deployment. This paper seeks robust, small models by pruning randomly initialized binary networks. The parameters begin at either +1 or −1 and remain fixed; learning selects a subnetwork structure that withstands adversarial attacks.

The approach therefore searches for useful connectivity within the initial network. It prunes different layers adaptively, uses a binary initialization scheme, and adds a final batch normalization layer to improve training stability. Together, these design choices produce compact networks with competitive performance. The authors interpret the results as confirming the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis under adversarial attacks and extending it to binary networks.

In the reported experiments, the method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art robust binary networks used for comparison. On some datasets, it also achieves higher accuracy than full-precision models. The paper additionally examines structured patterns in the pruned networks. These findings support the possibility of obtaining robust models through subnetwork selection with fixed binary parameters, while keeping the full-precision comparison specific to the datasets where it holds.
neurips-2022-robust-binary-models-by-pru.tldr: Pruning fixed, randomly initialized binary networks produces compact adversarially robust models that outperform robust binary comparisons in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models produce data from Gaussian noise by following a reversed stochastic process. Numerically simulating that process often requires many small time steps. This paper analyzes how ill-conditioning of the score contributes to that computational burden and explains why generation at multiple scales can accelerate it.

The explanation uses wavelets, which represent information at different scales. The data distribution is factored into conditional distributions of wavelet coefficients across those scales. The resulting Wavelet Score-based Generative Model synthesizes the coefficients using the same number of time steps at every scale, giving a computational structure whose time complexity grows linearly with image size.

The paper proves this behavior mathematically for Gaussian distributions and demonstrates it numerically for natural images and physical processes at phase transitions. Those two forms of evidence have different scopes: the Gaussian case carries the mathematical proof, while the broader data types supply numerical support. The contribution provides both an explanation of multiscale acceleration and a wavelet-based model that puts that explanation into practice.
neurips-2022-wavelet-score-based-generat.tldr: Wavelet-based conditional generation explains and enables faster score-based sampling, with linear image-size scaling proved for Gaussian distributions and supported numerically elsewhere.

paragraphs: Deep learning's success on images and text does not automatically establish its advantage on tables. This paper compares standard and newer neural approaches with tree-based models, including XGBoost and Random Forests. It defines 45 datasets across varied domains and evaluates both fitting models and searching for effective hyperparameters.

The benchmark finds that tree-based methods remain state of the art on medium-sized tabular datasets of roughly 10,000 examples. This holds even before taking their speed advantage into account. The authors then investigate the different inductive biases of trees and neural networks: the tendencies that make certain patterns easier for each model family to learn.

Their empirical analysis identifies three challenges for tabular neural architectures: handling uninformative features, preserving data orientation, and learning irregular functions easily. These are proposed directions for closing the observed gap. The released benchmark and detailed hyperparameter-search results provide a basis for subsequent comparisons. The paper's conclusion concerns the studied tabular regime and supplies concrete architectural questions alongside the performance evidence.
neurips-2022-why-do-tree-based-models-st.tldr: A 45-dataset benchmark finds trees ahead on medium-sized tabular data and identifies three learning challenges for tabular neural networks.
